    Step 3
    Deployment & handoff
    Production code, not a PDF

title: Corporate Credit Early Warning
text:
The business question
When a large company files for judicial recovery, the losses land on banks, bondholders, credit funds and the suppliers who sold to it on credit. Oi filed twice, in 2016 and 2023. Americanas filed in January 2023, days after it disclosed an accounting inconsistency. Light followed in May 2023. After each case a credit committee asks the same question: was there something in the public record, a year earlier, that should have changed the decision?
Since January 2025 the question also has a regulatory form. CMN Resolution 4,966 asks Brazilian lenders to provision for expected loss: the next 12 months for exposures in good standing, the whole remaining term once credit risk has increased significantly. That needs a probability of default for each horizon, not a single score, and it needs to notice the increase early.

title: Corporate Credit Early Warning
text:
The data
Everything is public. Quarterly and annual statements of every listed company come from the CVM open-data portal, each dated by the day it reached the regulator, so the model only sees what an analyst could have seen at the time. The auditor’s report is read for the going-concern paragraph. Material facts, the filings a company must publish when something relevant happens, carry the early news: a debt renegotiation, a covenant waiver, an asset sale to raise cash, a CFO who leaves. Interest rates, inflation, activity, unemployment and corporate default come from the Central Bank.
The hard part is the outcome. No public table lists when each listed company entered judicial or out-of-court recovery; the registry shows only the current status. The event base was rebuilt from three public traces (the registry, the filings of companies in recovery and the material facts that announce a filing), with a language model separating the company’s own filing from a customer’s or a subsidiary’s, and then checked by a second model that reads the filings of each event, under a fixed rule. It holds 106 events in 89 companies since 2011.

title: Corporate Credit Early Warning
text:
Method, and why this one
One panel, one test, eight models. Each listed non-financial company contributes one row per quarter, with what was known at the end of that quarter. Firms that left the market without an event stay in the data until they leave, so the sample does not keep only the survivors. The models go from the classical to the recent: the Altman score in its version for emerging markets, a discrete-time hazard logit, a Cox model, XGBoost as a classifier and as a survival model, a random survival forest, DeepSurv and DeepHit. All are trained up to 2018, skip 2019, and are tested from 2020 on, a period none of them saw.
Survival models, because the regulation asks for curves. A survival model gives the probability of default at 12, 24 and 36 months for every company and quarter, which is what lifetime expected loss needs. Whether those probabilities are calibrated, and not only whether they rank companies well, is tested separately.
Language models read the filings, and are tested like any other variable. A model reads the subject of each of about 31,000 material facts and marks eleven kinds of distress, with the company’s registered name, trade name and tax number hidden so it cannot recall how the story ended. A second model reads a sample to measure agreement, and 200 documents were read in full to see what the subject line misses. The test of whether these signals add anything was written down and committed before the test period was opened.
A credit memo that cannot invent a number. Agents assemble a memo for a credit committee: one reads the recent filings, one writes. A checker that is not a language model compares every number and date in the draft with the values the tools returned, and blocks the memo if one has no source.

title: Corporate Credit Early Warning
text:
Result
Corrected on 23 November 2026. An independent review of the code, after the first version went live, found errors that changed published results. The rule that reads the auditor’s going-concern paragraph also matched a standard sentence that every audit opinion carries since 2016, and the first memo on Casas Bahia wrongly cited such a paragraph. The calibration check kept unfinished windows only when they ended in a filing, which overstated the observed rates. The code was fixed, each fix with a test, and the whole test was run again; the hypotheses and the registered test did not change. The paper opens with an erratum that lists every correction and the conclusions that changed.
Version 2, 24 November 2026. A second pass fixed limits that the corrected version declared. The masking of company names cut other words (the name Oi inside “apoio”) and let trade names such as GPA through; names are now hidden as whole words, trade names included. The 1,055 subjects affected were read again and every result that uses the signals was run again: no conclusion changed. The version also adds what the plan promised and the first run left out: a table of what drives the risk and a test of the change of audit firm.



AUC of the 12-month PD for each model on the out-of-time test, with 95% intervals. The three tree ensembles are in red; the dashed line marks the Altman score.


Out of time, from 2020 on, the tree ensembles rank companies best: XGBoost survival and a random survival forest reach an AUC of about 0.85 for the 12-month PD, against 0.79 for the Altman score and 0.82 for the hazard logit. They beat the Altman score even when whole companies are resampled together; their edge over the hazard logit, a well-specified benchmark, is not significant under that test. On the level of risk, at 36 months the observed rate is 2.9% and most models overestimate it, with XGBoost survival closest. The curves need recalibration on the lender’s own defaults before they feed a provision.
The signals read by the language models did not improve the registered test: an AUC of 0.798 with them and 0.816 without. The treatment of extreme values had erased the five rarest kinds of signal; a run with them kept, decided after the test was opened, gives 0.819, no gain either. Read from subject lines, these signals do not add to the accounts.
What moves the risk is mostly in the accounts. In the XGBoost model, interest coverage, working capital over assets and recent losses weigh the most; in the Cox model, losses, a going-concern paragraph, negative equity and late filing raise the hazard, and working capital and cash lower it. A change of audit firm in the past year, tested after the test period was opened and so only as an exploration, added nothing significant to any model.
Memos on four past cases, written with what was known a year before each filing, show the reach and the limit. Casas Bahia came out with a 12-month PD of 3.3%, about three times the average. Americanas, whose problem sat inside its own statements, came out below the average.

section: What the literature has and has not done
text:
What the literature has and has not done
A systematic review under the PRISMA 2020 protocol screened 4,019 studies and included 1,642. Survival models appear in 96 of them, and only one study combines survival models with language models. Of the 59 studies with Brazilian data, one uses a survival model and none uses deep learning or a language model. Most abstracts do not say how the models were validated, and reading 60 of the studies in full does not change the picture much: 32 of them still do not say how the test set was formed, and only 10 check whether their probabilities are calibrated, which is what a provision depends on. The paper sets out the protocol, the counts and the gaps.

Case Study 06 · Live




RAG · Postgres + pgvector · Full-text search · Rank fusion · FastAPI · 22 tests

title: Hybrid RAG with a Numeric Guardrail
text:
The business question
A health plan’s member service answers the same questions all day. How long do I have to appeal a denied claim? What does the emergency room cost? How many telehealth visits are free? The answers are in the member handbook, and an assistant can find them in seconds.
It has to get one thing right every time: the number. A wrong co-pay or a wrong deadline is the expensive mistake, because the member acts on it.
Two things have to hold. The assistant finds the right passage even when the member uses different words than the handbook. And it refuses to answer when it is about to state a number the handbook does not contain.

title: Hybrid RAG with a Numeric Guardrail
text:
The data
A fictional health plan handbook with 8 documents: appeals, dental, emergency care, maternity, mental health, out-of-network care, prescriptions and telehealth. It is split into 21 passages. It is fictional on purpose. The repository is public, and a real plan’s documents are not mine to publish. The structure is the one that matters in a real handbook: limits, co-pays and deadlines.
The test set has 16 questions written in different words than the handbook: “ER” where the text says “emergency room”, “therapy” where it says “therapist”. Each question records which document answers it, so retrieval gets a score.

title: Hybrid RAG with a Numeric Guardrail
text:
Method, and why this one
One Postgres table instead of a vector database. Each passage is a row holding its text, its embedding (pgvector, HNSW index, cosine distance) and a full-text column with its own index. Re-loading a document is a delete and an insert in one transaction, so the two searches never see different versions of it. For most companies this means no new system to run, because Postgres is already there.
Two searches, combined by rank. Vector search finds paraphrases. Full-text search finds exact terms, codes and names. Their scores live on different scales, so instead of tuning a weight on 16 questions they are combined with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which only looks at each passage’s position in the two lists.
The guardrail fails closed. Before an answer goes out, every number in it is checked against the passages that were retrieved ($1,500.00 and 1500 count as the same number). If one is missing, the service returns no answer, flags it as blocked and names the number. For limits, co-pays and deadlines, no answer is cheaper than a wrong one.
It runs without an API key. A simple extractive answerer, which picks the best sentence from the passages, lets the whole pipeline and its tests run offline. A hosted language model gives the real answers when a key is set. In the same spirit, a deterministic embedder keeps the tests repeatable, and the evaluation then runs again with a real embedding model, bge-small-en-v1.5.

With a weak embedder, the hybrid beats both searches, because each one fixes misses of the other. With a good embedder, vector search already gets all 16 right and the hybrid keeps that. Full-text alone misses the paraphrases. Sixteen questions make a smoke test. The CI gate (at least 0.8 with the top 3 passages) is there to catch regressions when the chunking, the indexes or the query change.
The guardrail, as the tests check it. Ask “How long do I have to appeal a denied claim?” The handbook says 180 days, the answer says 180 days, and it cites the appeals document. Causal inference · Backdoor adjustment · Propensity weighting · Python


  Every number and every chart on this page comes from

title: Causal Modeling of NPS
text:
The business question
A company runs a customer-success programme — a proactive call to accounts that look like they need help. Six months in, the accounts that got the call have a visibly better Net Promoter Score. Leadership wants to expand the programme.
Should they? The dashboard shows a gap. It does not show whether the programme caused the gap, or whether the team simply called the accounts that were already going to be happy — the big ones, the long-tenured ones, the ones with few complaints. Expanding a programme on the strength of that gap can burn a budget on something that does nothing.

title: Causal Modeling of NPS
text:
The data
Simulated: 6,000 accounts, each with a size, a tenure, a support-ticket count, whether it received the intervention, and an NPS score.
The confounding is deliberate, and it is the whole point. In the simulator, bigger and longer-tenured accounts are both more likely to receive the call and happier to begin with. That is exactly the structure that makes a raw comparison misleading, and it is what real customer-success data looks like.
Why synthetic is the right choice here, not a compromise. With client data nobody reading this page could check whether the causal estimate is correct — the true effect is unobservable, which is the whole difficulty of the field. Here the true effect is a constant written in the code. That makes the estimator gradeable: you can see whether it recovers the answer, and by how much it misses.

title: Causal Modeling of NPS
text:
Method, and why this one
The naive comparison, for reference. Difference in mean NPS between treated and untreated accounts. This is what a dashboard reports, and it is the number the decision would otherwise rest on.
Backdoor adjustment. Regress NPS on the intervention while conditioning on the variables that drive both the intervention and the outcome — size, tenure, ticket count. Blocking those paths leaves the causal effect.
Propensity weighting. Model the probability of receiving the call given the same covariates, then weight each account by the inverse of that probability. This rebuilds a population in which treatment is as good as randomly assigned, and it makes a different set of assumptions than the regression — so agreement between the two is informative, and disagreement would be a warning.
Two estimators rather than one, on purpose. A single causal estimate is a claim; two that rest on different assumptions and land in the same place is evidence.

title: Causal Modeling of NPS
text:
Result



Effect of the intervention on NPS, three ways. The dashed line is the true effect, which is known here because the data was generated. Synthetic data — not client results.


The true effect written into the simulator is 0.80 NPS points.
The raw comparison reports 1.41 — it overstates the programme by roughly three quarters, because it is crediting the intervention with the head start of the accounts that received it. A team that expanded the programme on that number would find the returns quietly failing to materialise.
Both causal estimators land at 0.84, within their confidence intervals of the truth, and they agree with each other despite resting on different assumptions.
The point is not the decimals. It is that the gap between 1.41 and 0.80 is the difference between a programme that justifies its budget and one that mostly re-labels customers who were already loyal — and no amount of extra dashboard filtering would have revealed it.

Code
The script generates the data, runs all three estimators and produces the chart above. It is self-contained and deterministic — same seed, same numbers:

Requires numpy, pandas, statsmodels and matplotlib. Change EFEITO_VERDADEIRO at the top and rerun: the naive estimate moves with the confounding, the adjusted ones follow the truth.

Case Study 02 · Doctoral research




GAMLSS · Bayesian MSGARCH · Rolling-origin validation · R

title: Commodity Price Forecasting
text:
The business question
A grain buyer does not only need to know where the price is heading. They need to know how wrong that number could be, and whether being wrong costs the same in both directions.
Most forecasting stops at the first question. A cooperative deciding when to sell, or a processor deciding how much to hedge, is really asking the second one.

title: Commodity Price Forecasting
text:
The data
Public series only: agricultural commodity prices from international exchanges and Brazilian domestic markets, daily, over several years, with the exchange rate as the bridge between them. No client data is involved at any point.

title: Commodity Price Forecasting
text:
Method, and why this one
The usual simplification. Standard volatility models let the spread of returns move over time but hold everything else fixed — the asymmetry and the tail weight are treated as constants. In agricultural markets that assumption is uncomfortable: a drought does not widen the distribution symmetrically.
Letting the whole distribution move. GAMLSS gives each parameter of the distribution — location, scale, skewness, kurtosis — its own model with its own covariates. The shape of the distribution becomes something estimated over time rather than assumed.
Regimes, not gradual drift. Grain markets do not slide smoothly from calm to turbulent; they switch. Markov-switching GARCH estimates the states and the transition probabilities between them, and a Bayesian treatment carries the parameter uncertainty forward instead of collapsing it into a point estimate.
Validation that respects time. A model tuned on the full sample will always look good. Rolling-origin evaluation refits at each step using only what was knowable at that moment, and every added layer has to earn its place against simpler benchmarks — a plain GARCH, an ARIMA, a random walk. A more elaborate model that does not beat the simple one is a finding, not a failure.

title: Commodity Price Forecasting
text:
Result
Deliberately not published here. The manuscripts behind this work are under peer review, and putting their results on a personal website before the journals have ruled on them would be poor practice — and unfair to the reviewers reading them.
What can be said is the shape of the work: this is one stage of a doctoral thesis on multi-period, multi-objective portfolio optimisation in agricultural commodity markets, where distributional modelling feeds regime-switching volatility, which feeds scenario simulation, which feeds the optimisation layer. Each stage stands as its own manuscript.
Whatever of this line reaches print is listed on the research page, alongside the conference papers that already carry proceedings links. The case below is the part that is public and running today.

title: Multi-Agent Commodity Analyst
text:
Case Study 01 · Live




LLM Agents · MSGARCH / GARCH / ARIMA · Python orchestrates, R models · 167 tests

title: Multi-Agent Commodity Analyst
text:
The business question
What is corn and soybean price volatility telling us — and can a language model write that analysis without inventing a single number?
The second half is the harder one. A model that hallucinates a plausible figure in a commodity report is worse than no report at all, because the figure looks right.

title: Multi-Agent Commodity Analyst
text:
The data
Daily settlement prices from CBOT via Yahoo Finance: corn (ZC=F), 2,007 observations, and soybeans (ZS=F), 2,009 observations, both from 2 January 2018 to 30 December 2025. The USD/BRL rate (BRL=X) comes along, because analysing Brazilian domestic grain prices without the exchange rate is simply wrong.
Everything is frozen in a parquet cache with a metadata sidecar recording where each series came from. Two consequences: the published chart does not change on its own when the market moves, and the end-to-end test runs with no network.
The domestic CEPEA series is not implemented in this version. Rather than hide that, the collector falls back to the international series and the report prints the source swap above the chart. A system that states what it could not get is worth more than one that quietly substitutes.

title: Multi-Agent Commodity Analyst
text:
Method, and why this one
The agents do not know econometrics. Four of them — Collector, Econometrician, Critic, Writer — decide which function of the core to call and with which arguments. The core is plain, deterministic, testable Python and R. When the agent framework ages, the shell gets replaced and the part that matters stays.
Python orchestrates, R models. The model ladder is MSGARCH → GARCH → ARIMA, called over subprocess with a JSON contract. No rpy2, deliberately: it is the number-one source of installation pain in R+Python projects, and the goal was that anyone can clone and run. As a bonus, the R script runs standalone in RStudio when a model needs debugging.
The Critic rejects, with a written reason. It runs Ljung-Box and ARCH-LM on the residuals. Failure is not a silent retry — it is a rejection with a stated cause, capped at three attempts, backing down the model family each time.
The guard. The Writer cannot put a number in the text that does not exist in the results object. An invented number fails the run. The guard’s limits are documented in the repository too — it verifies digit provenance, not semantic meaning — because a case study that oversells its own safety net defeats the purpose.

title: Multi-Agent Commodity Analyst
text:
Result
The interesting outcome is not the forecast. It is that the critique loop fired in production, not in a test: in both commodities the Critic rejected MSGARCH — the signature model of my doctoral work — and approved GARCH on the second attempt.
For corn, ARCH-LM returned p = 0.0405; for soybeans, p = 0.0242. Both below 0.05, both meaning heteroskedasticity the model had not captured. The report says so, names the family, and gives the reason.



Corn (ZC=F), 2018–2025. The system produced this chart and the report beside it, from the frozen cache, with no network and no API key.


On the backtest, honesty matters more than a good-looking number: over a 20-step horizon the model scored MAPE 1.75% for corn — identical to the random walk. That is not a failure, it is arithmetic. Volatility models fix the mean at zero by construction, so the point forecast ties with a random walk by definition. Their contribution lives in the interval width and the residual diagnostics, and the system’s own report explains this without being asked.

title: Multi-Objective Portfolio Optimization
text:
Case Study 03 · Doctoral research




NSGA-II · Differential Evolution · Pareto frontiers · Multi-period

title: Multi-Objective Portfolio Optimization
text:
The business question
Which basket of commodity positions should a desk hold, when the decision has to satisfy several goals at once that genuinely conflict — and when the answer has to hold up over successive periods, not just today?
The convenient move is to blend the goals into a single score and optimise that. It produces one number and hides the judgement inside the weights, which is exactly the judgement the decision-maker was supposed to make.

title: Multi-Objective Portfolio Optimization
text:
The data
Public agricultural commodity price series, multi-period, plus the volatility and scenario structures produced by the forecasting stage. No client data, no proprietary feeds.

title: Multi-Objective Portfolio Optimization
text:
Method, and why this one
Keep the trade-off open. Rather than one optimum, evolutionary multi-objective algorithms return a Pareto frontier: the set of portfolios where improving one objective necessarily costs another. The decision-maker chooses a point on that frontier knowing what the choice costs, instead of inheriting a weighting someone else picked.
More than two objectives. With three or more competing criteria the problem becomes many-objective, where the usual algorithms degrade in ways that are easy to miss. That makes the choice of algorithm a research question rather than a default — NSGA-II and differential evolution do not behave the same way, and comparing them properly needs a benchmark designed for the multi-period commodity setting rather than borrowed from elsewhere.
Regimes change the answer. A frontier estimated in a calm market is the wrong frontier for a turbulent one. Conditioning the decision on the estimated market regime, and refining it with dynamic programming across periods, ties the optimisation back to the volatility modelling upstream instead of treating it as a separate exercise.
What survives contact with reality. A strategy that is optimal on paper can be impossible to execute at size. Capacity limits, turnover and generalisation across several assets are part of the problem statement here, not an afterthought.

title: Multi-Objective Portfolio Optimization
text:
Result
Deliberately not published here. These manuscripts are under peer review or being prepared for submission. Publishing their results on a personal site ahead of the journals would be poor practice, so the frontiers, benchmark tables and comparisons stay out of this page until the papers are out.
The one exception is work that is already public: a conference paper comparing NSGA-II and differential evolution on multi-objective portfolio optimisation was presented at ICPR Americas 2024, and a second on Pareto frontiers built across multiple time windows is in the ConBRepro proceedings.

title: Framework or Hand-Rolled?
text:
Case Study 05 · Live




LangGraph · StateGraph · Parity testing · 173 tests

title: Framework or Hand-Rolled?
text:
The business question
A team is about to build an agentic system. Someone asks whether to adopt an agent framework or write the orchestration by hand. The honest answer is it depends — which helps nobody.
So: take a multi-agent system that already works without a framework, rebuild its orchestration on LangGraph, and measure the difference instead of arguing about it.

title: Framework or Hand-Rolled?
text:
The setup
The subject is the multi-agent commodity analyst from case study 01 — four agents over a deterministic econometric core in R, with a critique loop and an anti-hallucination guard.
The rule that makes the comparison mean anything: only the orchestration changes. The four agents and the whole agro/ core are imported, not rewritten. The hand-rolled version is a for loop with a break; the LangGraph version is a StateGraph with five nodes and two conditional edges.
Switching between them is a flag:
python run.py --commodity milho --pergunta "..." --fake-llm --engine manual
python run.py --commodity milho --pergunta "..." --fake-llm --engine langgraph

title: Framework or Hand-Rolled?
text:
Method, and why this one
Parity first, opinions later. Six tests run both engines on the same input and compare the results field by field: chosen model family, number of attempts, the rejection history, the residual diagnostics, the backtest, the set of numbers the guard authorises — and the final markdown.
Without that, “I reimplemented it in LangGraph” is a claim. With it, it is a property. And a reimplementation that behaves almost the same is worse than none at all: it looks like an alternative and is actually a trap.
The agents did not become tools. LangGraph offers ToolNode and the ReAct pattern, where the model decides which tool to call next. That is not what this system does. The order — collect, fit, critique, write — is fixed on purpose, and the LLM chooses parameters, never the next step. Turning fit_model into a tool would have been a change of semantics disguised as a change of framework, and the comparison only holds if both sides do the same thing.

title: Framework or Hand-Rolled?
text:
Result
The reports are byte-identical. Same SHA-256, end to end, from the frozen cache:
manual   : 94488AF71916321F4CE51258547E01F8BB4F9E43D43FBCE8238C20BF0543DCF0
langgraph: 94488AF71916321F4CE51258547E01F8BB4F9E43D43FBCE8238C20BF0543DCF0
What the framework charged. MemorySaver — the checkpointer, and the main reason to adopt LangGraph at all — serialises the state at every node with msgpack. A pandas.Series is not serialisable, so the first version of the graph failed outright:
TypeError: Type is not msgpack serializable: Series
The hand-written loop never meets this, because there the series is a local variable read once. To keep checkpointing, the state had to carry only the data bundle — a dataclass of primitives holding a file path — and every node that needs the series re-reads it from disk.
Measured at runtime: 1 parquet read in the manual engine, 3 in the graph. Total time barely moved, because the bottleneck is the R subprocess, not the disk. At this data size the cost is real and irrelevant. On a large series it would stop being irrelevant, and the choice would be to drop the checkpointer or write a custom serialiser.
What the framework bought. Pipeline state stops being implicit in local variables and becomes a declared TypedDict. The rejection loop becomes a conditional edge you can read without tracing control flow in your head. And the checkpointer lets you inspect and resume a run mid-execution — something the hand-rolled loop does not offer.
The price in code: 54 lines of code hand-rolled against 120 in the graph, for identical behaviour.
So which one? For this system, the hand-written loop wins: the pipeline is short, the control flow fits on one screen, and nothing here needs resumability. The framework would start paying for itself with more branches, human-in-the-loop pauses, or runs long enough that resuming matters. That is a conclusion drawn from a measurement, not from taste — and either way, the parity tests mean switching costs a flag.

title: Framework or Hand-Rolled?
text:
Code
github.com/rhozon/commodity-agents
Both engines live in the same repository: agents/orchestrator.py and agents_langgraph/graph.py, with tests/test_paridade.py holding them to the same result. The suite is 173 tests, and it runs with no API key and no network.
langgraph and langchain-core are in requirements.txt, but only the graph engine and the parity test import them — the import is deferred, so the default engine needs neither.

title: Forecasting Hospital Admissions
text:
Case Study 07 · Live




Time series · Seasonal ARIMA · Rolling-origin backtest · 80% bands checked for coverage · Python · 19 tests

title: Forecasting Hospital Admissions
text:
The business question
Beds, nursing shifts, supplies and the budget behind them are committed months in advance, and all of them depend on one number: how many patients will be admitted. A state health department, a hospital network and a health plan all face it.
The usual answer is last year’s figure for the same month, adjusted by feel. It is simple, and it is a fair benchmark. The question here is how much better a model does on months it has not seen, and whether the range around its forecast can be trusted when someone sizes a team on it.

title: Forecasting Hospital Admissions
text:
The data
Public data from DATASUS: every hospital admission paid by SUS, Brazil’s public health system, counted by state and month from January 2008 to September 2026. That is 27 series, and about 1.2 million admissions a month for the country as a whole.
The same admissions can be counted by the month the patient was admitted or by the month the hospital’s bill was processed. The first looks like the obvious choice. For the latest months it is wrong, because hospitals send their records late:



The same admissions counted two ways, Brazil, January 2025 to September 2026. By month of admission, the last three months are 7%, 19% and 43% short, because those records are still arriving.


A model fitted on that line would see demand collapsing in the third quarter of 2026. Nothing collapsed; the paperwork was late. The forecast uses the processing month.
The processing month has its own flaw: now and then a state’s batch does not arrive. Acre shows zero admissions in August and September 2026, and Roraima drops from about 4,000 a month to 517 and then to zero. Those are missing records, not missing patients.

title: Forecasting Hospital Admissions
text:
Method, and why this one
Missing data is called missing. A month below 60% of the median of the previous 12 is treated as a batch that never arrived and left out. The rule looks only at the past, so it works on the most recent month. It flags 9 months in 3 states.
The pandemic is left out of the fit. From March 2020 to December 2021 elective care stopped and then caught up. Those months describe a shock, not the seasonal pattern the forecast has to reproduce, so the model skips them as if they were missing.
A simple model, with the calendar as its only outside input. Seasonal ARIMA on the log of admissions, the specification known as the airline model, with the number of working days in each month as a regressor. Elective admissions happen on working days, and a February with Carnival has two fewer of them than one without. The calendar is known in advance, so the forecast can use it honestly. Adding it cuts the error over the first three months from 2.82% to 2.62% of the volume.
Tested the way it would be used. At each of 33 dates, from January 2023 to September 2025, the model is refitted on the data available at that date and forecasts the next 12 months, for every state. That gives 891 twelve-month forecasts to score. The benchmark goes through exactly the same test. Each decision above has its own variant in the test, so its effect is measured rather than assumed.
The error measure is WAPE: total absolute error divided by total admissions. It reads as “off by X% of the volume”, and small states do not dominate it.

Over the first three months the error falls by more than half, from 6.0% to 2.6% of the volume. The model beats the benchmark in all 27 states. For the 12-month total, the figure a budget is built on, the typical error is 2.7% against 4.5%, and in the worst tenth of cases 7.0% against 9.1%.
The bigger difference is in the range around the forecast. A band labelled 80% should contain the actual value about 80% of the time. With the pandemic left in, the model learns that the world can fall apart at any moment. Its band ends up 15% to 27% of the forecast wide and contains the actual value 87% to 96% of the time. A plan sized on that band carries beds and staff it will not need. With the pandemic left out, the band is 10% to 16% wide and contains the actual value 80% to 83% of the time, which is what it promises.
The forecast for the next twelve months, Paraná as an example:



Paraná, monthly admissions and the forecast for October 2026 to September 2027 with its 80% band. The shaded years were left out of the fit.


About 1.16 million admissions over the twelve months, 3.8% more than in the previous twelve. The repository has the same forecast for every state.
The limits are part of the result. Small states are hard for every model: Roraima and Amapá stay above 16% error. State totals are the right level for a health department, while a hospital needs the same pipeline on its own cut of the data. And the pandemic window was set by hand. A shock of that size would call for the same decision again.

Applied to your data
This is the Custom Forecasting package on public data: admissions here, and in your case demand, claims, exams or default. The steps are the same: find what in the data is a recording artifact, beat a simple benchmark on months the model has not seen, and deliver a band that holds what it promises.

title: Dynamic Pricing for Ride-Hailing
text:
Case Study 09 · Live, 25 November 2026




DuckDB · XGBoost · Choice models · Natural experiment · Evolutionary game theory · Switchback design · Python · 13 tests

title: Dynamic Pricing for Ride-Hailing
text:
The business question
A ride-hailing platform sets a price for every area and every hour. Two populations answer it, and neither answers at once. Riders compare the app with its rival, and with not riding at all. Drivers look at what each part of the city paid yesterday and decide where to work today. A price that clears the market this evening changes where the drivers will be tomorrow, and that changes the price the platform will need then.
So the useful questions are dynamic. How much of the fare is the trip and how much is the market? How many requests will each zone get next week? How fast do riders switch apps when one becomes cheaper? And does the price that looks best today make supply and waits swing later? The same questions apply to any business that prices a perishable capacity under moving demand: car rental, delivery, parking, hotels, events.

title: Dynamic Pricing for Ride-Hailing
text:
The data
Every trip is public. New York’s Taxi and Limousine Commission publishes each Uber and Lyft trip with the time of the request and of the pickup, the zones, distance, time, the fare before fees, the driver’s pay, and since 5 January 2025 the congestion fee. This case reads 15 months, 301.6 million trips (December 2023 to April 2024, and September 2024 to June 2025), with DuckDB, one pass per month, in about a minute for the whole set.
A quality report runs on every month. It found what the documentation does not say: the time the car arrived is missing for 99.7% of Lyft trips until February 2025, and is filled only from March 2025 on, so the wait used here is pickup minus request, which exists for every trip; about 1% of trips have a pickup before the request and are left out of the waits.
The natural experiment comes from the platforms themselves. When the congestion fee started, Lyft credited riders the $1.50 fee on rides in the zone, from 5 to 31 January 2025, each credit valid for a week. Uber did not. The fee hits both apps alike inside the zone; the credit made Lyft cheaper there for about five weeks.

title: Dynamic Pricing for Ride-Hailing
text:
Try it
The simulator below uses the estimates of this case. Change the price in an area and hour and see trips, revenue, the platform’s margin and the wait. Switch to the adaptation tab to see riders and drivers react day after day under three pricing policies, or plan an experiment.

title: Dynamic Pricing for Ride-Hailing
text:
Method
A fare model that separates the trip from the market. A log-linear base fare on distance, time, app and airport explains 79% of the variance of log fares. What is left, averaged by area and hour, is a dynamic price index. An XGBoost model with place and time on top shows how much a full pricing model gains.
A forecast made a week ahead. Trips per zone and hour for 253 zones, with only what is known a week before: calendar, holidays and lags of one to four weeks. Each test month, April to June 2025, is forecast by a model trained on everything before it, against two baselines: the same hour last week and the mean of the last four weeks.
Riders as an evolving population. The Lyft share among Uber and Lyft trips that start in each zone of the congestion zone is followed day by day. Three nested choice models compete: static choice, where the share depends only on today’s prices and waits; a logit dynamic with inertia, where the share moves part of the way toward that target each day; and replicator-like drift, where it never comes back. The inertia parameter decides between them. The credit is measured by difference in differences against zones outside the congestion zone, and the same calendar a year earlier, when there was no credit, serves as placebo.
Drivers as a second population, in a simulator. Six areas, calibrated on Lyft’s weekday evening peak from February to June 2025. Each day drivers move toward the areas that paid more than usual, by an exponential replicator whose speed is the one thing the public data cannot pin down, so it is varied. The wait responds to demand per driver with an elasticity of 0.21, estimated within zone and hour of the week. Riders follow the choice model above. The demand elasticity, -0.4 with a range of -0.2 to -0.6, comes from published estimates for Uber (Cohen et al., 2016). Three policies face a lasting 25% rise in demand in the congestion zone: a fixed price, a surge that clears the market every day, and the same surge smoothed.
An experiment the platform could run. Price policies interfere across riders and drivers, so a rider-level A/B test is biased. The planner uses switchback blocks and the observed variability of the hourly margin to give the smallest effect a test can detect.

title: Dynamic Pricing for Ride-Hailing
text:
Results
The fare. Out of sample, in June 2025, the base fare misses by 23.4% on average (mean absolute percentage error) and the full XGBoost model by 18.3%. Trips that start in the congestion zone cost 5% to 39% more than the same distance and time would cost on average, depending on the hour, highest late at night; in the Bronx, Queens and Staten Island trips run at 0.84 to 1.02 of that level.
The forecast. A week ahead, the XGBoost model’s error (WAPE) averages 13.1% over the three test months, against 16.1% for the same hour last week and 13.0% for the mean of the last four weeks. The four-week mean is a hard benchmark at this horizon, and the model only ties it.
The riders. The data choose the middle model. The daily inertia is 0.61 (95% interval 0.58 to 0.64): the share closes about 39% of the gap to its target each day, a half-life of about 1.4 days. Relative price and wait matter as expected: one extra minute of Lyft wait against Uber lowers Lyft’s log-odds share by 0.08. The credit, however, left no measurable mark. Inside the zone, Lyft’s share rose by 0.021 in log-odds during the credit (interval -0.002 to 0.045), but the same weeks a year earlier, with no credit, show 0.029. Forecasting 8 February to 30 April 2025, the dynamic model is not more accurate than the static one (share error of 2.83 against 2.80 points). Riders adapt, but within days, and a five-week credit did not move them for good.
The drivers and the price policy. With slow drivers the three policies settle, and the market-clearing surge earns 4.6% more margin than a fixed price with a shorter wait. The surge, though, makes drivers’ relative pay move with the multiplier itself, which amplifies their reaction about 2.5 times. Cycles start at an imitation speed of 0.75 under the clearing surge, at 1.75 when it is smoothed to a tenth of the gap per day, and between 1 and 2 with a fixed price. When prices cycle, the margin can even rise, because short-run demand is inelastic, while waits grow and drivers crowd in and out of the same areas. A platform that looks only at the margin will not see the cost; riders and drivers will.
The experiment. With four-hour blocks the log margin of a block varies around its usual level with a standard deviation of 0.22, so two weeks detect a 15% change in margin, four weeks 10%, eight weeks 7%. Since drivers keep moving after a switch, the dynamics above argue for blocks long enough to let them settle.

title: Dynamic Pricing for Ride-Hailing
text:
Limits
Prices are what the platforms chose, so the price coefficients are associations given zone, day of week and wait, not causal elasticities; the causal part of the case is the credit, and there the effect is not distinguishable from the placebo. Credits and promotions do not appear in the fares, and Uber’s own promotions are unknown. Daily inertia may mix habits with persistent local shocks. The simulator assumes the observed split of drivers is a rest point, uses a published elasticity, and has no driver identifiers, so its speeds are scenarios, not estimates. In 2025 Uber started passing some requests to yellow cabs, which leave this data.

title: Dynamic Pricing for Ride-Hailing
text:
Applied to your pricing
This is the Custom Forecasting package applied to price. For a mobility or delivery platform, a car rental or fleet operator, a parking or events business, it becomes a pricing engine with three parts: a demand forecast by place and hour, a price response measured on your own data, and a policy tested in a simulator and then in a switchback before it goes live. The decision on prices stays with your people.

Recommendations · PyTorch · Implicit ALS · Segmentation · Imputation · Assortment optimization · Uplift modeling · PySpark · Python · 25 tests

title: Recommendations and Promotions for a B2B Wholesaler
text:
The business question
A wholesaler that sells through an ordering platform serves thousands of small retailers. Each week it has to decide what to put in front of each one: the products it reorders, the ones it has never tried, the shelf a whole group of similar shops sees first, and which retailers get a promotion that costs money. Part of the orders also arrive without an account number, and those sales vanish from every customer history built on top of them.
This case answers the five questions on one public data set, with the same rule for all of them: every model learns from the past and is scored on a period it never saw.

title: Recommendations and Promotions for a B2B Wholesaler
text:
The data
Online Retail II (Chen, 2012, UCI Machine Learning Repository, CC BY 4.0) holds every invoice line of a UK online seller of gift-ware from 1 December 2009 to 9 December 2011: 1,067,371 lines, 39,516 sale invoices, 5,852 customers in about 40 countries and 4,707 products. The data set notes that many of its customers are wholesalers, which makes it one of the few public B2B order logs.
It is also messy in the ways real order data is, and each problem is counted before anything is modeled. 19,494 lines are cancellations; 34,335 are exact duplicates, 22,844 of them because the two sheets of the workbook both contain 1 to 9 December 2010; 6,093 carry codes that are not products (postage, bank charges, manual adjustments); 6,207 have a zero or negative price; 7,881 have a price more than ten times above or below the usual price of the same product, and are kept but flagged. After cleaning, 1,003,214 sale lines remain.
The largest gap is the customer: 22.6% of the sale lines, 13.1% of the revenue, have no customer number.

title: Recommendations and Promotions for a B2B Wholesaler
text:
Method, and why this one
One cutoff for everything. Models learn from the orders before 9 October 2011 and are scored on the last 61 days. Their settings were chosen on the 61 days before that, so the test window was used once. 12.5% of the revenue in the test window comes from products never sold before the cutoff, which no model here can recommend.
Two recommendation tasks, not one. For a wholesaler, most of the next order repeats past orders. Recommending “what you already buy” and “what you have never bought” are different jobs, and they are scored separately. Five models compete: popularity in the last 90 days, “buy again”, item-to-item co-purchase, implicit ALS, and a sequential model in PyTorch that reads each customer’s orders in sequence with a GRU and scores every product for the next order. Each recommendation shows the customer’s own product it is most often bought with, so a sales rep can explain it. Scores are Recall@10 and NDCG@10 with 95% bootstrap intervals over customers.
Segments that a manager can name. Customers are grouped by recency, frequency, revenue, basket size and range of products, with k-means and the number of groups chosen by silhouette. The names come from the medians of each group.
Imputation evaluated, not assumed. To see whether orders without a customer number can be attributed, the number is hidden on orders where it is known, and each basket is matched to the purchase profiles of known customers in the same country.
A shelf with variety. For each segment, a mixed-integer program picks the 30 products with the highest recent segment revenue with at most 4 from any product family (families come from the product descriptions, since the data has no category). It is compared with the segment’s top sellers and the overall top sellers on what the segment bought in the test window.
Promotions on a semi-synthetic experiment. The data has no promotions, so a randomized voucher is simulated on the real customers: each customer’s spend without the voucher is the real spend in the test window, and the voucher’s effect is a known function of the customer’s real history (it brings back lapsed customers who used to spend, and gives away a discount to frequent buyers who would have ordered anyway). Because the true effect is known for every customer, any targeting rule can be scored exactly. This measures whether uplift models find who responds; it does not show how this wholesaler’s customers respond to real promotions.
Spark, with a parity test. The cleaning rules and an implicit ALS are also written in PySpark. CI runs them on a sample of the raw file and fails if Spark and pandas disagree on any sale line.

Most of the next order is a reorder. Scored on everything customers bought in the test window, the simplest rule wins by far: offering each customer its own most frequent products (“buy again”) reaches an NDCG@10 of 0.341, against 0.260 for the sequential model, the best of the learned ones. Orders without a customer number should not be attributed automatically. With the number hidden on the 4,790 orders of the test window, the basket matching puts the right customer first 22.5% of the time and in the top ten 46.3% of the time, among customers seen before, against 4.4% and 11.1% for the busiest customers of the same country. It narrows the search, but even its most confident quarter of matches is right only 24.1% of the time, and 12.2% of the orders come from customers never seen before. The orders without a number also look different: the typical one has 20 lines against 15, at a typical unit price of £3.36 against £1.97, which points to another sales channel rather than known accounts that did not log in. The pipeline keeps them out of the customer histories and turns the matches into a review queue: in the test window, 29 of the 227 orders without a number reach the confidence of the top quarter.
A shelf with variety holds up where it matters. For the top segment, the optimized shelf of 30 products covered 12.6% of what those customers bought in the test window and reached 76.8% of them, against 11.6% and 72.6% for the segment’s top sellers and 11.9% and 72.3% for the overall top sellers, with 12 product families instead of 7 and 9. In the two lapsed segments the cap costs a little revenue coverage (8.1% against 8.5%, and 4.5% against 4.9%). In every segment, the shelf that covers the most revenue is one built for that segment.
Promotion targeting: the models pay off on small budgets. In the simulated voucher test on the 5,472 customers with history (10 replications), giving the voucher to the 20% of customers the X-learner ranks highest brings £39,590 of true incremental revenue, against £21,940 for random targeting, £23,488 for the top spenders and £23,892 for the most lapsed customers; an oracle that knows every effect would reach £102,578. Learning who responds is hard because spend varies by orders of magnitude between customers. Dividing the outcome by each customer’s past monthly revenue before fitting, which keeps the estimate unbiased under random assignment, raised the X-learner’s area under the gain curve from 13% to 23% of the oracle’s.
Over the whole range of budgets, the rule “most lapsed first” still covers the most area, 45% of the oracle’s, because the simulated effect was built around lapsed customers and the rule happens to match it. With an effect twice as large the X-learner reaches 41%; with four times as large, the three learners on the scaled outcome pass the rule (the X-learner reaches 61%). For a real campaign: a randomized test on about 5,500 customers already pays off when the budget is small and targeted; ranking the whole base needs a larger effect or a larger test.

The data covers one seller of gift-ware in 2009 to 2011, mostly in the UK; the numbers are evidence about the methods, not about any other company. Products launched in the test window cannot be recommended by any of these models; a content-based model on product attributes would be the next step. The Spark job runs locally in CI on a sample; it has not run on a cluster.

title: Airline Pricing and Competition in Brazil
text:
Case Study 11 · Live, 25 November 2026




Industrial organization · Natural experiments · Instrumental variables · Logit demand · Bertrand-Nash · Merger simulation · Python · 7 tests

title: Airline Pricing and Competition in Brazil
text:
The business question
Three airlines carry almost every domestic passenger in Brazil. When a carrier leaves a route, how much do the fares of those who stay go up? When a new one arrives, do the incumbents cut prices? And if two of the three merged, which routes would pay for it, and how much? In January 2025 Azul and Abra, the controller of Gol, signed a memorandum to study a combination that would have held about 60% of the domestic market; the talks ended in September 2025, with Abra saying the idea still had merit. The question is alive for regulators, airports, travel buyers and the carriers themselves.

title: Airline Pricing and Competition in Brazil
text:
The data
ANAC, the civil aviation agency, publishes every domestic fare sold to the public each month and how many seats were sold at it. This case reads 89 months, January 2019 to May 2026: 42.7 million fare lines and 217.9 million seats. The files changed header, encoding and decimal mark several times; the loader reads them all and a quality table records each one. ANAC’s traffic statistics add paid passengers, seats offered, fuel burned, distance and departures for every route, carrier and month. Fares are deflated by the IPCA to 2025 reais.
Two limits come with the source. The fare files cover public sales only, about 27% of paid passengers; corporate deals, miles and free tickets are not in them, so the fare is the price of a public ticket, not the average revenue per passenger. And a market here is an airport pair, so Congonhas and Guarulhos are different markets.

title: Airline Pricing and Competition in Brazil
text:
Try it
Pick one of the 60 busiest routes. See each carrier’s fare, passengers and the cost and margin the model implies; start a price war and watch the rivals answer; merge two carriers; or let a low-cost entrant in. The price sensitivity can be set to the central estimate or to either end of the range the specifications give.

title: Airline Pricing and Competition in Brazil
text:
Method
Natural experiments first. Avianca Brasil collapsed in the first half of 2019; ITA flew from mid-2021 until it stopped in December 2021. Each event is measured by difference in differences on the fares of the carriers that stayed: routes where the event carrier had a meaningful share against routes it never served, with carrier-route and month fixed effects, passenger weights and errors clustered by route.
Demand with instruments. Passengers choose a carrier on the route or not to fly it, in a logit model (Berry, 1994) estimated on 164 routes and 392 carrier-route products from January 2022 to May 2026. Fixed effects for each carrier on each route absorb lasting quality, and month effects absorb seasons. Price is endogenous: fares rise when demand is strong, which is why ordinary least squares finds almost no response to price. The instruments shift price without moving this route’s demand: the same carrier’s fare per kilometre on its other routes that month (a Hausman-type cost instrument), the number of carriers on the route and the rivals’ frequency.
Competition as a game. Each carrier sets its fare to maximize profit given the others’, a Bertrand-Nash equilibrium with differentiated products. Its first-order condition gives the margin each carrier must have and, from the observed fare, the marginal cost it implies. A merger changes who owns what, an exit removes a carrier, an entry adds one; new equilibria are found by iterating the first-order conditions.
A test before the forecast. Before simulating a merger, the model is asked to predict the fares that followed Avianca Brasil’s exit, using only the first quarter of 2019.

title: Airline Pricing and Competition in Brazil
text:
Results
When Avianca Brasil left, rivals’ fares spiked, then settled a little higher. On the 50 routes where it had at least 10% of passengers, the fares of those who stayed rose 15% in April, 22% in May and 19% in June 2019 against control routes, while flights were cancelled and seats disappeared. From July to December the difference was 3.0% (95% interval -3.0% to 9.3%), not distinguishable from zero.
ITA’s year is too short to say much. On the 9 routes where it had at least 5% of passengers, rivals’ fares moved 6.8% while it flew (interval -17% to 38%) and 21.9% in the months after it stopped (interval -6% to 58%). The direction fits the story; nine routes cannot confirm it.
Price matters once it is instrumented. Least squares gives a price coefficient of 0.034 per hundred reais, which would make every carrier’s demand inelastic. With the instruments the coefficient is 0.276 (standard error 0.048, first-stage F of 154), and the median carrier faces an own-price elasticity of -1.35. The estimate depends on the instruments: adding a fuel-cost shifter gives 0.285, treating frequency as given gives 0.171, the Hausman instrument alone gives 0.036, and the overidentification test rejects in every case with several instruments. A nested logit that would let carriers be closer substitutes for each other than for not flying gave a nesting parameter below zero, outside the model, so the plain logit is used. The simulator lets the visitor move between 0.171 and 0.285.
The model passes the Avianca test. Removing Avianca Brasil from the first-quarter 2019 equilibrium, the model predicts a 3.3% rise in the fares of those who stay, against the 3.0% observed in the second half of the year. With the lowest price sensitivity it predicts 5.2%. The observed interval is wide, so this is a consistency check, not a proof.

title: Airline Pricing and Competition in Brazil
text:
Limits
The fare is the public-sale fare, a minority of passengers. The model sees monthly averages, so it ignores how fares change as departure approaches and how carriers manage seats. The instruments disagree with each other, which the overidentification test shows; the range of results is reported rather than hidden. Costs come from the pricing model, not from accounts: they are positive for 77% of carrier-routes, and margins look large (a median of 75% of the fare), which says the marginal cost of one more passenger on a scheduled flight is small, not that the airlines are profitable. Mergers also change networks, frequencies and costs, which this model holds fixed.
